name: Poly Network
technique: Cross-chain message called privileged keeper function

rootCause: EthCrossChainManager would execute any cross-chain message against any contract, including EthCrossChainData, which stored the keeper public keys. The attacker brute-forced a function name whose selector collided with putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes and replaced the keepers with their own key. Most funds were returned.

Poly Network, a cross-chain interoperability protocol, said it was attacked, and a total of more than 610 million US dollars were transferred to 3 addresses. Among them, the funds transferred to Binance smart chain addresses starting with 0x0D6e2 exceeded 250 million US dollars, and they were transferred to the ether starting with 0xC8a65. There are over 270 million U.S. dollars in workshop addresses, and over 85 million U.S. dollars in transfers to Polygon addresses. Affected by this, the large amount of assets in the O3 Swap cross-chain pool was transferred out, and the official is investigating.With the efforts of many parties, the hackers have now returned tokens worth 342 million U.S.…

Poly Network suffered a $611M exploit on August 10, 2021, when an attacker used a cross-chain message to replace the bridge's validator set, gaining full withdrawal authority and draining funds from Ethereum, BSC, and Polygon. The flaw was an unprotected call path in the EthCrossChainManager contract, which let arbitrary calls change critical admin keys. All stolen funds were later returned. The EthCrossChainManager contract processed arbitrary cross-chain calls without restricting the destination contract or function, allowing an attacker to send a crafted message that called putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes on EthCrossChainData and replaced the validator set with their own key.

On August 10, 2021, Poly Network’s cross-chain bridge was exploited for approximately $611 million across Ethereum, Binance Smart Chain, and Polygon. The attacker abused a flaw in cross-chain message handling to seize validator control, then drained bridge assets. Poly Network’s EthCrossChainManager contract permitted cross-chain messages to instruct it to call arbitrary methods on arbitrary contracts, including privileged admin functions. The manager was owner of EthCrossChainData, allowing an attacker to update keeper (validator) keys and seize control without proper access restriction.
